dimensions.gloss: How much of the output the AI produced, expressed as a degree or a level on a named ordinal scale.
A bare 'type' dimension named alongside stage and degree in one sentence, with no example values to show whether it means type of AI tool, of task, or of contribution.
dimensions.note: Kept as its own singleton rather than folded into AI tool identity or purpose of AI use, because the quote does not give enough context to know which it means.

dimensions.gloss: A named taxonomy of the ways AI output can diverge from truth or intent (hallucination, sycophancy, confabulation, inherited bias, strategic deception).
variants: a five-part taxonomy of ai output divergence

dimensions.gloss: Which AI tool, product, or model was used, whether named directly or reported as present/absent.
Which version or build of the AI tool was used.
An open remarks field accompanying a structured AI-use declaration.
A named four-pillar framework of AI governance controls across the mobile software development lifecycle.
variants: four pillars across the mobile sdlc

dimensions.gloss: A named four-principle foundation for human-AI collaborative work (source verification, human authority, openness, continuity).
A named five-stage conceptual model for assessing and guiding responsible AI use, with no stage content given.
Whether the human's own purpose or goal for the AI interaction was clearly articulated.
The quality or discipline with which prompts and context were constructed to steer the AI.
Whether and how rigorously a human checked, verified, curated, or edited the AI's output.
Whether the human maintained independent judgment rather than deferring to the AI.
Whether personal or sensitive data was protected during the AI interaction.
Which actor in a chain (developer, vendor, institution, practitioner) bears responsibility for an AI-related outcome.
A named 8-domain risk-calculator/triage tool for AI use, referenced without its component domains.
A named six-domain taxonomy of where a scheme's stated requirements mismatch its underlying assumptions (capability claims, categorization, prohibited uses, confidentiality, disclosure, attribution).
A named four-stance editorial policy matrix organizing permissible AI use by material contribution and confidentiality risk.
The forms of evidence (staged work, oral explanation, live demonstration, provenance, programme mapping) that should be triangulated to assess a contribution.
What criteria or roles qualify a person as an author or contributor, as defined by a named authorship-criteria system.
dimensions.note: Groups several distinct, named, competing authorship-criteria systems (CRediT, ICMJE, COPE, WAME, CSE, NIH, McNutt et al.) that different papers cite to answer the same underlying question of who counts as an author or contributor.

dimensions.gloss: A specific item drawn from a named published reporting checklist or guideline (CLAIM, TRIPOD, SPIRIT-AI) that a study or protocol should address.
dimensions.note: Each item is a line from a different named guideline; grouped because all three play the identical structural role of a checklist row.

dimensions.gloss: A software design requirement that AI actions be identifiable, attributable to provenance, and logged.
A software design requirement that AI autonomy be bounded and steerable by policy.
A software design requirement that AI action remain subject to human oversight and interruption.
A software design requirement that AI components interoperate with the wider platform ecosystem.
Whether a coded task was performed by the GenAI tool or by the human developer.
The nature of the relationship (e.g., involvement in design, funding, analysis, or data collection) between a conflicting or sponsoring entity and either the study or an individual author.
dimensions.note: Same source scheme applies the same relationship-type axis at two levels (study-level and author-level); grouped as one axis measured at two units of analysis.

dimensions.gloss: A named set of reporting domains (validity, reliability, fairness, integrity, transparency, human oversight) that an AI reporting framework covers.
A five-point scale scoring overall compliance with FAIR data principles.
Whether shared data and metadata are in a standard, machine-readable, open format (the FAIR 'I' criterion).
Whether shared data carry a reusable format, an open licence, and accompanying reproduction code (the FAIR 'R' criterion).
The structured set of role and responsibility sections used in a team contributorship or collaboration agreement.
variants: another grid to reflect the literature synthesis process
dimensions.note: The second grid is introduced in its source as 'another grid' alongside the first, so this may be two components of one instrument rather than two independent schemes; grouped together as a close call.

dimensions.gloss: The named type of inappropriate or unethical authorship practice (honorary, gift, guest, coercive, ghost, anonymous, paid, denied).
A named step-by-step author guidance for describing, identifying, and citing physical samples in open research.
variants: publishing open research using physical samples: guidance for authors

dimensions.canonical_label: Stage/location of AI use in the work process
dimensions.gloss: At which point, section, or research-process stage the AI was applied, as distinct from what it was used for or how much it did.
variants: the sections of the manuscript where genai was applied
dimensions.note: Combines a generic 'stage' term with two concrete operationalizations (manuscript section; CRediT-like research stage) on the judgment that all three answer 'where in the process,' not 'where the disclosure statement itself sits' (kept separate as disclosure-location-placement).

dimensions.gloss: What task or function the AI was used for, e.g., language editing, content generation, decision-making, or productivity.
variants: the purpose of genai use (eg, language editing or content generation)
dimensions.note: Merges cross-scheme paraphrases from research-publishing and government sources. 'AI usage patterns' is one of two axes in a single government classification scheme (paired with 'AI usage domains,' kept separate as sector/domain), so folding it in here is a judgment call.

dimensions.gloss: The dimension (causal, moral, or legal) along which responsibility for an AI-related outcome is attributed.
variants: three dimensions of the attribution of responsibility

dimensions.gloss: The factors (control, participation, fault management) proposed to counter diffusion of responsibility in human-AI systems.
The specific type of AI-related incident recorded, e.g., secondary data use, safeguard bypass, or data breach.
Whether specific types of AI use are explicitly designated as permitted or prohibited.
variants: are any types of ai use explicitly permitted or prohibited?
dimensions.note: One label is an actual instance of a prohibited-use list, the other a coding question asking whether such a specification exists; both concern the same permitted/prohibited axis.

dimensions.gloss: Whether any statement disclosing a contribution or an AI use was included at all, regardless of what it is disclosing.
dimensions.note: Treated as one general presence axis usable for any disclosure subject, rather than splitting by subject matter (contribution vs. AI use).

dimensions.gloss: Where in the document the disclosure statement appears, or whether guidance specifies where or how it should be declared.
variants: are there guidelines on where or how ai use should be declared?
dimensions.note: The guideline item also bundles 'how' (manner) together with 'where,' so this is a partial fit onto a pure location axis.

dimensions.gloss: Whether the disclosure follows, or is guided toward, a standardized or suggested reporting format (e.g., the CRediT taxonomy).
variants: is there a suggested format for declaring ai use?

dimensions.gloss: Whether the article explicitly states that no AI tools were used, as distinct from simply lacking any statement.
Whether a journal or institution has a guideline or policy requiring a given type of disclosure.
variants: presence of guidelines on reporting author contributions
presence of guidelines on ai use

dimensions.gloss: A named six-question journalistic framework (who, what, when, where, why, how) applied wholesale as a coding lens.
The top-level thematic category assigned in a qualitative coding of AI-related questions or concerns.
The finer sub-category nested within a top-level qualitative theme.
The type of AI-related misconduct underlying a retraction, e.g., fabricated text, fabricated data, fabricated images, peer-review manipulation, or non-disclosure.
The estimated probability that a specified harm scenario will occur.
The estimated magnitude of consequence if a harm scenario occurs.
The composite risk tier produced by cross-tabulating likelihood and severity.
The banded level (high/medium/low) into which a numeric EAS score is grouped.
The recommended governance action (encourage, permit with oversight, restrict, prohibit) that follows from a risk assessment.
Who, by role or position, is typically involved in a given inappropriate-authorship practice.
Whether a given AI-use scenario is judged ethically acceptable, contingent on whether it was disclosed.
The access tier (unrestricted, non-commercial, contributor-controlled) applied to a shared dataset.
Introductory or contextual boilerplate content at the start of an AI transparency statement document.
A statement defining the meaning, scope, or boundaries of 'AI' as used by the disclosing agency.
The sector or domain (service delivery, compliance, law enforcement, policy, science, corporate) in which the AI is applied.
Whether and how the AI system directly or indirectly affects members of the public.
The organizational measures in place to monitor deployed AI systems and protect the public against negative impacts.
Whether the disclosure references compliance with applicable external regulations.
Metadata about the disclosure document's publish date or update frequency.
Contact information provided for public enquiries about the disclosure.
The category of LLM involvement in conceptual or intellectual tasks such as idea generation, structuring, and critical analysis.
The category of LLM involvement in language-level tasks such as editing, clarity, style, and translation.
The category of LLM involvement in research-process tasks such as question refinement, search strategy, literature retrieval, and data preparation.
The named metadata fields defined by the Citation File Format schema for describing software.
